In our prior study, we showcased using aCD117/tLNP-Puma mRNA for in vivo HSC depletion,3 which could overcome the adverse side effects associated with conventional approaches (i.e., chemotherapy, radiation).

Despite the potent depletion of HSCs with aCD117/tLNP-Puma, this agent also caused toxicity due to off-target uptake by the liver.23 We hypothesize that incorporating CD47 modification on the aCD117/tLNP-Puma would diminish Puma-induced liver toxicity while retaining its HSC depletion function (Figure 3A).
To explore this hypothesis, we first asked whether CD47 modification could reduce the liver uptake of aCD117/tLNP-mRNA while preserving its ability to target the BM.
We injected 1 μg of aCD117/tLNP-Luc or CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Luc in the mice and then imaged luciferase biodistribution in the liver and whole-femur BM using IVIS.
In the absence of HSCs-targeting element aCD117, CD47 modification potently reduced liver expression of luciferase (CD47+immunoglobulin G (IgG)/tLNP vs.
IgG/tLNP), but without luciferase expression in the BM.
When aCD117 was added to the surface of LNPs, CD47 modification not only reduced luciferase expression in liver but also enhanced expression in the BM (Figure 3B).

Conjugating cell-targeting antibodies to LNP-mRNA to yield tLNP-mRNA has been demonstrated as an effective approach for tissue- or cell-specific delivery of mRNAs.2,3,11,12,18,19 As CD47 modification reduces liver uptake, we hypothesize that incorporating CD47 modification into tLNPs (CD47/tLNP-mRNA) could augment targeted delivery of mRNA.

To evaluate tissue specificity and in vivo targeting efficiency of CD47/tLNP-mRNA, we sought to target lung endothelium using anti-CD31 antibody, as previously reported.11 First, anti-mouse CD31 antibody was conjugated to CD47/LNP-Luc (Figure 2A).
Then, we performed IVIS bioluminescence imaging of harvested tissues from mice treated with 10 μg aCD31/tLNP-Luc or CD47+aCD31/tLNP-Luc.
The CD47-modified LNP-Luc group demonstrated a boosted luciferase expression in the lung and a reduced expression in liver and spleen (Figures 2B and 2C).
To quantitatively assess the difference of tissue uptake of tLNP with vs.

without CD47, we measured the luciferase activity per milligram protein in the desired organs and found lung-specific luciferase expression increased from 1.5E+6 LU/mg protein in the unmodified group to 2E+6 LU/mg protein in the CD47-modified group, demonstrating a ∼33% enhancement; in contrast, liver and spleen uptake was significantly reduced in the CD47-modified group (Figure S2).

To assess whether elevated lung uptake reflects an enhanced delivery to the lung CD31+ endothelial cells, we injected 1 μg aCD31/tLNP-ZsGreen or CD47+aCD31/tLNP-ZsGreen into the mice i.v.; then, we harvested and dissociated lungs 24 h post-treatment to measure ZsGreen expression in CD45−CD31+ endothelial cells.

mRNA-based therapeutics delivered via lipid nanoparticles (LNP-mRNA) hold great promise for treating diverse diseases.

However, further improvements are needed to refine outcomes in non-vaccine, extrahepatic applications, such as minimizing the rapid clearance and off-target uptake in undesired tissues of the mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS).

We propose modifying LNP surfaces with the phagocytic cell “don’t eat me” signal, CD47, in combination with our previously established antibody-based targeted LNP (tLNP) to create a CD47/tLNP platform with reduced phagocytic clearance and off-target effects and improved efficiency for cell-specific delivery.
We showed that CD47 modification decreased macrophage and hepatic uptake both in vitro and in vivo.
Combining CD47 modification with antibodies targeting endothelial cells, T cells, or hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) increased targeting efficiency up to 3-fold compared to tLNP alone.
Enhanced targeting of CD47/tLNP to HSCs with reduced off-targeting enabled the delivery of pro-apoptotic mRNA for HSC depletion as a preconditioning strategy prior to bone marrow transplant.
Additionally, CD47-modified LNPs showed diminished inflammatory effects on hepatic tissue and an altered protein corona.

Our CD47/tLNP-mRNA platform, with its reduced phagocytic clearance, mitigated inflammatory effects, and enhanced targeted delivery, should further facilitate the development of in vivo mRNA therapeutics.

Lipid nanoparticle encapsulating messenger RNA (LNP-mRNA) has emerged as a promising tool for therapeutic gene delivery in applications such as in vivo chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell production and in vivo hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) gene editing.1,2,3 However, despite the tremendous success of LNP-mRNA technology for vaccine applications, this system still faces challenges in achieving sufficient dosages for extrahepatic applications in vivo, largely due to the innate immune response and phagocytic uptake of LNP-mRNA by cells of the mononuclear phagocytic system (MPS).4 Furthermore, while LNP-mRNA are still in the bloodstream, they naturally bind to serum proteins such as apolipoprotein E (ApoE) to form a protein corona, which promotes their uptake by the liver hepatocytes through the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) classical pathway.5,6 Although beneficial for hepatic delivery of therapeutics,7,8 this liver tropism poses a challenge for efficient delivery of LNP-mRNA therapies to non-liver cells in vivo.
We first modified the surface of LNP-mRNA with CD47 peptide to generate CD47/LNP-mRNA (Figure 1A).
To assess CD47 peptide grafting density on LNPs, we first determined the total particle count in 1 μg (by mRNA) of CD47/LNP-mRNA as 7.5E+11 using the ZetaView TWIN instrument.
We then measured the average CD47 peptide content via the ultra-sensitive CBQCA protein quantification assay.
The number of CD47 peptides per LNP was calculated as 8.9 (±0.5), and the grafting efficiency was calculated as 89.4% (Figure S1).

To assess whether CD47 peptide incorporation would alter the physical properties of LNPs, we compared the particle size, polydispersity index, and zeta potential of LNP encapsulating green fluorescent protein (GFP) mRNA (LNP-GFP) with vs.
without CD47 peptide modification, using a Malvern Zetasizer.
Interestingly, the zeta potential of CD47-modified LNPs is slightly closer to neutral (2.72 ± 1.82 vs.

−6.88 ± 0.52), which may be a benefit to less non-specific interactions with blood components.13,14,15,16 To examine the potential of CD47/LNP-mRNA to evade phagocytic uptake in vitro, we delivered unmodified LNP-mRNA, CD47/LNP-mRNA, or SIRP-α blockade + CD47/LNP-mRNA, where the mRNA encoded GFP (LNP-GFP), to the SIRP-α expressing mouse macrophage cell line RAW 264.7.17 The SIRP-α blockade was performed by incubating the cells with 20 μg/mL SIRP-α blockade antibody in full medium for 2 h at 37°C before the LNP treatment.

At 24 h after treatment, we imaged the cells and found that cells transfected with CD47/LNP-GFP showed a substantial decrease in GFP expression, suggesting that CD47 modification reduced macrophage uptake of LNP-mRNA (Figure 1C, two center panels).
The reduction of GFP expression was partially reversed by SIRP-α blockade (Figure 1C, right panel).
Further quantitative analysis with flow cytometry showed that while CD47 peptide incorporation significantly reduced GFP mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) by 75% (6,419 vs.
24,841 relative fluorescence units [RFU]), SIRP-α blockade rescued this reduction (13,032 RFU) (Figures 1D and 1E).

In parallel, to test whether CD47 modification can enhance delivery of aCD4/tLNP that targets CD4+ T cells,2,11,20,21,22 we first injected 10 μg aCD4/tLNP-Luc or CD47+aCD4/tLNP-Luc into the mice i.v.
and then measured luciferase expression in the liver and spleen.
We found enhanced mRNA expression in the spleen and reduced mRNA expression in the liver in mice injected with CD47+aCD4/tLNP-Luc (Figures 2F and 2G).
To directly evaluate the T cell-targeting efficiency of CD47-modified tLNP, we injected 1 μg CD47+aCD4/tLNP-ZsGreen or unmodified aCD4/tLNP-ZsGreen into the mice i.v.
and harvested the spleen 24 h after the flow cytometry analysis of ZsGreen expression in T cells.

Mice treated with aCD4/tLNP-ZsGreen showed an average of 46.6% ZsGreen+ in CD4+ T cells, which increased to 51.1% with the addition of the CD47 peptide (Figures 2H and 2I), indicating that CD47 modification enhances CD4+ T cell targeting.
In summary, these data suggest that co-decorating antibody-modified targeted LNP with CD47 peptide have the potential to enhance the efficiency of targeted delivery.

Micelles containing the CD47 peptide were incorporated into LNPs via post-insertion mixing.66 LNPs were decorated with monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) specific for mouse CD4, CD31, CD117, IgG isotype control, and/or CD47 peptide for further experiments.

To prepare targeted LNPs, purified rat anti-mouse CD4, clone RM4-5 (BioLegend), purified rat anti-mouse CD31, clone MEC13.3 (BioLegend), purified rat anti-mouse CD117, clone 2B8 (BioLegend), or purified rat IgG isotype control (Thermo Fisher) mAbs were coupled to LNP-mRNA via N-succinimidyl S-acetylthioacetate (SATA)-maleimide conjugation chemistry, as described previously.1,3,11 Briefly, LNP-mRNA or CD47/LNP-mRNA was modified with maleimide functioning groups (DSPE-PEG-mal) by a post-insertion technique.
The mAb was functionalized with SATA (Thermo Fisher) to introduce sulfhydryl groups, allowing conjugation to maleimide.

To further assess how CD47 modification affects LNP-mRNA biodistribution and protein expression, we generated CD47-modified LNP-luciferase mRNA (CD47/LNP-Luc) for in vivo imaging system (IVIS) bioluminescence analysis.
injected with 10 μg unmodified LNP-Luc or CD47/LNP-Luc.
Four hours later, the organs were harvested and prepared for imaging (Figure 1I).
In the CD47-modified group, the liver showed a ∼3-fold decrease in luciferase activity, and the spleen showed a ∼2-fold decrease, as measured by total flux photons per second (p/s) (Figure 1J).
These data suggest that CD47 modification reduces mRNA delivery and expression to the liver and spleen.

Cellulose-purified m1ψ-containing mRNAs were encapsulated using a self-assembly process described previously.65 Briefly, an ethanolic lipid mixture of ionizable cationic lipid, phosphatidylcholine, cholesterol, and PEG-lipid was mixed rapidly with an aqueous solution containing the mRNA at acidic pH.
The ionizable lipid is proprietary to Acuitas Therapeutics.
The mRNA-loaded LNPs were characterized by dynamic light scattering using a Zetasizer Nano ZS (Malvern Instruments) and a Quant iT Ribogreen assay (Thermo Fisher).
The mean hydrodynamic diameter of these LNP-mRNAs was ∼80 nm, with a polydispersity index of 0.02–0.06 and an encapsulation efficiency of ∼95%.

C57BL/6J mice were administered radiolabeled Na125I LNP-Luc.2,11,12 At T = 4 h post-injection, animals were euthanized, and selected organs (liver, spleen, lung, kidneys, and heart) were harvested, rinsed with PBS, or stored at −80°C until analysis.

It is known that LNP-mRNA in the bloodstream interacts with serum biomolecules to form a surface protein corona, which critically affects the clearance rate and biodistribution of the LNP-mRNA.14,40,41,42 To assess whether CD47 modification alters the protein corona, we analyzed the composition of the protein corona formed surrounding CD47/LNP-mRNA, control scrambled peptide/LNP-mRNA, or unmodified LNP-mRNA.
The LNP-mRNA variants were incubated with normal mouse serum at a 1:1 ratio for 1 h at 37°C.
We identified a total of 41 proteins that were differentially adsorbed among the LNP-mRNA groups (Figure 4D).
In the corona of CD47-modified LNP, apolipoproteins Apoa2 and Apoe were significantly less abundant, with an Apoe Z score of −0.04 in the CD47-modified LNP compared to 1.02 in the unmodified LNP.
The Apoe is known to promote hepatic uptake of LNP through binding to LDLRs on liver cells and facilitate clearance of LNP from the bloodstream into the liver.

In accordance, Apoc3 and Apoc4, which act as antagonists to Apoe and inhibit liver uptake of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins via LDLRs, were found to be elevated in the protein corona of CD47-modified LNP.44,45,46,47,48,49 Notably, CD47/LNP-mRNA also shows an increased affinity for serum albumin (Albu), the most abundant plasma protein that has been shown to increase the retention of LNPs in the bloodstream, with a Z score of 1.11 compared to −0.28 in unmodified LNP.
The decreased interaction with Apoe and increased binding to Albu may underlie the reduced liver uptake of CD47-modified LNP-mRNA, as shown in Figures 1F–1J.

Equal volumes of CD47/LNP, scrambled CD47/LNP, or unmodified LNP, in which the LNP was labeled with DiO fluorescent dye, were gently mixed with normal mouse serum (Thermo Fisher) for a total of 0.2 mL volume and incubated for 1 h at 37°C.
The 0.2-mL fractions positive for LNP as detected through fluorescence intensity (Figure S4) were pooled together, totaling 1.2 mL and frozen on dry ice.

Peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) recruitment is an indicator of inflammatory stimuli.24 To test whether CD47-modified LNP-mRNA are less inflammatory than unmodified LNPs, we compared PBMC counts in mice treated with either unmodified LNP-mRNA or CD47/LNP-mRNA after i.v.
We found that the PBMC counts from CD47/LNP-mRNA-treated mice are comparable to those of untreated mice (∼5E+6 vs.
∼3E+6 PBMC/mL).
In contrast, PBMC counts from unmodified LNP-mRNA-treated mice showed a 10-fold increase (∼3E+7 cells/mL) (Figure 4A) when compared to untreated mice.
These data indicate that CD47-modified LNP-mRNA are less inflammatory compared to unmodified LNP-mRNA.

Our previous work showed that LNP-mRNA administration exaggerates pre-existing inflammation.16 To further test whether CD47-modified LNP-mRNA are less inflammatory than unmodified LNP-mRNA, we treated mice with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to induce an inflammatory state, followed by the administration of CD47/LNP-mRNA or unmodified LNP-mRNA; then, we assessed the level of pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 (IL-6) in the serum.

To evaluate how CD47 modification affects the biodistribution of LNP-mRNA in vivo, we radiolabeled unmodified LNP-mRNA and CD47/LNP-mRNA with Na125I for particle biodistribution analysis (Figure 1F).
LNP-mRNA were administered i.v.
Four hours post-administration, tissues were harvested and prepared for radioactivity counting.
In per gram of blood, CD47/LNP-mRNA-treated mice showed a retention rate of ∼20% of the injected dosage (ID/g), compared to only about 4% ID/g in unmodified LNP-mRNA-treated mice.
Additionally, CD47/LNP-mRNA-treated mice exhibited a ∼6-fold decrease in liver uptake and a ∼3-fold decrease in spleen uptake compared to those treated with unmodified LNP-mRNA (Figure 1G).

LR measures the organ-to-blood ratio of LNP uptake, allowing for a comparison of biodistribution while accounting for differences in blood clearance.11,12 The LR of unmodified LNP-mRNA compared to CD47/LNP-mRNA was significantly higher in the liver by ∼23-fold and in the spleen by ∼11-fold (Mann-Whitney U test, ∗∗p < 0.01).
These in vivo results indicate that CD47 modification reduces hepatic and splenic uptake of LNPs.
Since unmodified LNP-mRNA mainly accumulates in the liver, we explored liver responses to CD47-modified LNP-mRNA by performing RNA-seq on liver samples from C57BL/6 mice 4 h after i.v.
administration of 10 μg unmodified LNP-mRNA, CD47/LNP-mRNA, or scrambled peptide/LNP-mRNA.

The differential gene expression analysis indicates a significant downregulation of 30 genes, ranging from −18.40 to −2.11-fold in CD47/LNP-mRNA-treated and untreated mice compared to unmodified LNP-mRNA-treated mice (Figure 4C).

Eight genes belong to the acute phase response (APR) pro-inflammatory protein family, including Saa3,25 Timp1,26 Plscr1,27 Cxcl9,28 Cd14,29 Hamp,30 Hpx,31 and Serpina10.32 Notably, the most differentially expressed gene, Saa3, which is downregulated by a fold change of −18.40 (p = 1E−7) in the CD47-modified group, is a murine APR apolipoprotein gene produced in hepatic or extrahepatic tissues and responds to systemic pro-inflammatory stimulation.33,34 Other genes, including Gbp2,35 Gbp6,36 Bmper,37 and Id1,38 involved in phagocytosis, autophagy, and endocytosis, were also significantly downregulated in the CD47-modified group.
Principal-component analysis39 showed that the CD47-modified group clustered close to the untreated mice compared to the unmodified LNP-mRNA group (Figure S3).
Together, these RNA-seq data indicate that CD47-modified LNP-mRNA reduces acute inflammatory responses in the liver.

LNP-mRNA platform technology may still face clinical barriers when it comes to systemic delivery of mRNA therapeutics.
This includes, but is not limited to, the high cellular uptake by the MPS and inherent preferential hepatic tropism.

Another barrier is the subsequent activation of the innate immune response that hinders the bioavailability of therapeutic mRNA cargo to the target cells.50,51 Therefore, improving LNP delivery to extrahepatic tissues is critical for mRNA therapeutic development.

tLNP has emerged as a promising mRNA delivery system for in vivo therapeutics and gene therapy, offering superior tissue and cell specificity.1,2,3,52,53,54 However, this system still suffers from off-target mRNA expression.

Here, we demonstrate that the surface decoration of LNP-mRNA with CD47 self-peptide, along with cell-targeting antibodies, substantially boosted mRNA delivery in three target cell types of interest in vivo—T cells, lung endothelial cells, and HSCs.

Our previous studies have demonstrated a wide spectrum of applications of antibody-targeted LNP-mRNA in gene therapy, such as in vivo CAR-T cell production, in vivo gene editing, and in vivo delivery of functional mRNAs to HSCs.1,3 This study describes a peptide-cloaked LNP-mRNA platform that incorporates a “don’t eat me” CD47 signal into LNP-mRNA.
This modification effectively reduces the non-specific uptake of LNP by the mononuclear phagocytic system and mitigates the pro-inflammatory aspects of LNP in vivo.

As a result, our platform significantly enhances the bioavailability of mRNA cargoes to the intended targeted cells, thereby improving the efficacy of mRNA delivery and reducing unwanted off-target effects.
The CD47/tLNP-mRNA platform presented here could pave the way for precise delivery of LNP-mRNA-based therapeutics across a broad spectrum of diseases.
We demonstrated in vivo that CD47/LNP-mRNA decreased hepatic uptake compared to unmodified LNPs.
We then tested the tissue-targeting capability of CD47/LNP-mRNA by co-conjugating with anti-CD31, anti-CD4, or anti-CD117 antibodies for systemic delivery.
We showed that the resulting CD47/tLNP-mRNAs led to significantly higher levels of mRNA delivery and expression in each target cell.
We then evaluated the potential of CD47+aCD117/tLNP-mRNA in HSC targeting and to switch on a Cre/loxP-mediated reporter system.

Through RNA-seq and serum pro-inflammatory cytokine analyses, we found that CD47/LNP-mRNA induces a lower pro-inflammatory response in hepatic tissue compared to non-modified LNP-mRNA; particularly the genes within the APR pathway were downregulated.
It is worthy of note that the CD47 modification also contributes to a 5-fold increase of LNP-mRNA presence in the bloodstream upon administration.

The data from the protein corona composition analysis of a corona surrounding CD47/LNP-mRNA indicate that such an increase may likely be attributed to the composition of its serum protein corona and reduced affinity for Apoe, an important protein for shuttling LNP-mRNA to the liver.55 We observed significantly increased targeting efficiency of CD47/tLNP-mRNA, including a 150% increase in lung targeting efficiency of CD47+aCD31/tLNP-mRNA over aCD31/tLNP-mRNA.
We also showed that CD47 modification enables a novel method of HSC depletion via the targeted delivery of cytotoxic Puma mRNA.

Current genotoxic conditioning regimen causes substantial pulmonary, liver, and reproductive toxicity.56,57,58 HSC depletion with CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma ameliorated the Puma-induced toxicity from non-specific uptake observed by aCD117/tLNP-Puma and empowered successful engraftment and hematopoiesis after BMT.
A beneficial aspect of the LNP-mRNA platform is the modular nature of LNP composition and surface modification.

For example, we have shown in previous work that LNP-mRNA can be conjugated with targeting antibodies to enable delivery to specific cell types in vivo following intravenous (i.v.) administration, such as HSCs,3 T cells,2 lung endothelium,11 and inflamed brain vasculature.12 We hypothesize that incorporating the CD47 peptide onto the surface of targeted LNP (tLNP)-mRNA will reduce their uptake and clearance by the MPS, alter the protein corona to minimize unwanted hepatic uptake, and thereby enhance the targeted delivery of mRNA to specific cell types.

Here, we report on the development and evaluation of CD47 peptide-cloaked LNP-mRNA (CD47/LNP-mRNA), which resulted in a substantial decrease in uptake of LNP-mRNA by the phagocytic system and a reduction in biodistribution in the liver.

We then examined the impact of CD47 modification of LNP on in vivo cell targeting by co-conjugating CD47/LNP-mRNA with antibodies targeting endothelial cells (CD47+aCD31/tLNP-mRNA), T cells (CD47+aCD4/tLNP-mRNA), and HSCs (CD47+aCD117/tLNP-mRNA).2,3,11 Through biodistribution experiments, we found a prominent expression boost in targeted tissues and a reduction in off-target effects in the liver.
We also demonstrated that CD47/LNP-mRNA evades pro-inflammatory pathways, as evidenced by RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) assays.
The presented immune-evasive CD47/tLNP-mRNA platform offers a promising tool for enhanced efficacy of targeted mRNA therapeutics.

We then tested in vivo HSC depletion with CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma as pre-conditioning for BMT.
The donor HSCs carry a permanent GFP reporter, enabling the evaluation of engraftment level by measuring GFP in blood cells.

Four months post-BMT, mice preconditioned with CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma resulted in prominently higher GFP expression in the CD45+, CD19+, CD3+, and GR1+ blood-derived monocyte populations, compared to those preconditioned with aCD117/tLNP-Puma (Figure 3G), suggesting a higher HSC depletion efficacy with CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma.

Nevertheless, the GFP+ cells constitute only a minor fraction (∼0.5%), which could be attributed to the incomplete depletion of the recipient’s HSC and the equal competence (if not higher) of the remaining recipient HSCs and the transferred HSCs.

Indeed, when we analyzed the percentage of GFP+ blood cells at a much earlier time point (2 weeks post-BMT) compared to the 4-month time point, we observed a higher percentage of GFP+ granulocytes (∼1.5%) and a comparable percentage of GFP+ red blood cells (RBCs) in mice preconditioned with CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma (Figure 3H).
In the future, the BMT regimen will be further optimized by increasing CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma dosage for preconditioning and the quantity of transferred HSCs.
Nonetheless, we demonstrated that CD47 modification is a promising strategy to reduce the Puma-induced liver toxicity by using aCD117/tLNP-Puma for preconditioning of BMT.

Following delivery into the bloodstream, the protein corona forms around the LNPs, allowing for increased uptake by the MPS and subsequent processing in the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes.9 The MPS consists of immune surveillance cells such as monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells, which engulf bacteria, dead tissue cells, and exogenous material.

MPS cells widely express the phagocytosis regulatory marker, signal regulatory protein-α (SIRP-α) on their surface.10 The anti-phagocytic counterpart of SIRP-α is transmembrane protein CD47, which is a recognition molecule acting as a ubiquitous “don’t eat me” signal found on cell surfaces.10
